cards.title: Something fishy
cards.body:
**Phishing** (said "fishing") is when a scammer sends a message pretending to be someone you trust, like your bank, your school or a game, hoping you'll bite: click a link, open a file or hand over your details.

The good news: most phishing messages have the same few warning signs, and once you know them, they're easy to spot.

cards.title: The warning signs
cards.body:
- **Fake sender:** the name looks right, but the email address isn't the real company's.
- **Rushing you:** "Act now!", "Your account closes in 24 hours!" Pressure stops you thinking.
- **"Dear Customer":** a real company that knows you usually uses your name. (Scammers sometimes find your name online too, so a name doesn't prove it's real.)
- **Asks for secrets:** passwords, sign-in codes, card numbers or PINs. Real companies never ask for these by email.
- **Hidden link:** a button or link that goes somewhere other than the real website.
- **Too good to be true:** prizes you never entered, free phones, easy money.

cards.title: Who really sent it?
cards.body:
Anyone can type any **name** into the From line. What counts is the **address after the @**.

A real company sends from its own [[domain name]]. If Your Bank's website is `yourbank.example`, its emails end in `@yourbank.example`. Something like `@yourbank-help.example` belongs to someone else: a [[lookalike domain]]. In a long address, the owner is the name **just before the ending**: `@yourbank.example.help-desk.example` belongs to `help-desk.example`.

To see where a link really goes **without opening it**, hover over it with a mouse, or press and hold it on a phone. Many mail apps also show it under the button.

cards.prompt: Your Bank's real emails come from **@yourbank.example**. Tap **every** warning sign in this email.
cards.explanation: Five warning signs: the sender's address isn't `@yourbank.example`, the subject is **rushing you**, it says **"Dear Customer"**, it **asks for secrets** (your password and card number), and the button goes to `yourbank-verify.example`. The date and the sign-off are normal.
cards.hint: Check each line against the warning signs: who sent it, how it talks to you, what it asks for, and where the button goes.
cards.nudge: There are five signs. Look closely at the address after the @, the subject line, the greeting, what it asks you to send, and where the button goes.

items.label: A link to a different site than it says
Your school's usual email about a trip

cards.explanation: Rushing, asking for secrets, prizes you pay to claim and links that go somewhere else are all phishing signs. A message from the **real** address that sends you to the official app, or a normal note from your school, is probably fine. If you're ever unsure, check another way.
cards.hint: Run each one past the warning signs: fake sender, rushing, "Dear Customer", asking for secrets, hidden links, too good to be true.
cards.nudge: A message is suspicious if it rushes you, asks for secrets, or offers a prize you pay for. A real address sending you to the official app is fine.

cards.title: What to do instead
cards.body:
- **Don't click** links or open attachments in a message you're unsure about, and don't reply.
- **Go there yourself:** open the official app, or type the address you know. If there's really a problem, you'll see it there.
- **Report it** with your mail app's "Report phishing" or "Junk" button, then delete it.
- **Ask a trusted adult** if you're not sure.

Already clicked or typed something in? Don't panic, and don't hide it: change that password straight away and tell a trusted adult. There's a whole module on what to do next.

cards.prompt: An email pops up while you're doing homework.

steps.text: **"Congratulations! You've won a games console! Click here within 1 hour to claim your prize."** You never entered a competition. What do you do?

choices.text: Click quickly, before the hour is up
choices.consequence: The rush is the trick. The link leads to a page that asks for your details or payment.

choices.text: Reply to ask if it's real
choices.consequence: Replying tells the scammer your address works, so you'll get more scams.

choices.text: Report it as phishing and delete it
choices.consequence: No prize is lost, because there never was one. Reporting helps your mail app catch the next one.

cards.explanation: A prize you never entered, plus a deadline, is a classic scam. **Don't click, don't reply**: report it and delete it.
cards.hint: Check it against the warning signs: did you enter a competition? Why is there a one-hour deadline?

cards.prompt: Label four of the warning signs in this email.
cards.explanation: The sender's address is a **fake sender**, the subject is **rushing you**, the message **asks for secrets**, and the button is a **hidden link** to `yourbank-verify.example`.
cards.hint: Match each label to a line: who sent it, the subject, what it asks you to send, and where the button goes.
cards.nudge: "Fake sender" goes on the From line, and "Hidden link" on the button. Then which line rushes you, and which asks for your password?

cards.prompt: Your Bank's website is `yourbank.example`. Which email address is **really** Your Bank's?

options.nudge: Read the ending: the name just before the final `.example` is `help-desk`, so `help-desk.example` owns this one.
`yourbank-alerts` is a different name from `yourbank`: that's a lookalike.
The part after the @ is what counts. `mail-alerts.example` isn't Your Bank.

cards.explanation: Only `@yourbank.example` is Your Bank. In a long address, the owner is the name **just before the ending**: `yourbank.example.help-desk.example` belongs to `help-desk.example`.
cards.hint: Look only at the part after the @, and find the name just before the final ending.

cards.prompt: An email arrives that seems personal.

steps.text: **"Hi Sam, your school account will be deleted today. Sign in here to keep it."** It uses your real name and school. What do you do?

choices.text: Sign in with the link. It knows your name, so it's real
choices.consequence: Scammers can find names and schools online. Using your name doesn't make it real.

choices.text: Don't use the link: sign in the usual way, or ask your teacher
choices.consequence: Your account is fine, and your teacher reports the scam to the school.

cards.explanation: A personal touch doesn't prove a message is real: scammers find names online. Check by going to the site **your usual way**, or by asking someone who'd know.
cards.hint: The warning signs said a name doesn't prove it's real. What's the safe way to check your account?

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- **Phishing** pretends to be someone you trust.
- Warning signs: **fake sender**, **rushing you**, **"Dear Customer"**, **asks for secrets**, **hidden links**, **too good to be true**.
- The **address after the @** is what counts, not the name.
- Don't click: **go there yourself**, report it, and ask a trusted adult.

Next: scams in text messages and phone calls.
